source.context_raw:
passage 1:Fertilize at the right time of year. In order to your fertilizer to work best, you'll need to time it so that you fertilize at the beginning of the growing season. This is different for different types of grasses. Fertilize warm season grasses when the grass begins to turn green at the beginning of spring.

passage 2:Picking Out Fertilizer. 1  1. Know your grass. The type of grass you have will determine what type of fertilizer you need to use, and how often you need to fertilize. 2  2. Do a pH soil test. This measures the alkalinity or acidity of the soil, and helps to determine what pH your fertilizer should have. 3  3. Measure your lawn.

passage 3:Pour in the rest of the fertilizer. Apply the rest of fertilizer in a perpendicular pattern. Step on the turf and if the leaf blade bounces back up, your lawn is in good shape. If it lays flat, you've over-fertilized.
source.query_raw: what is the proper way to fertilize your grass

open_questions.description: The term 'soil' is used in 'alkalinity or acidity of the soil' (context:span:10). While 'Soil Characteristic' captures properties, 'soil' itself might be a distinct physical entity. This question is resolved by adding CT-Soil.

The phrase 'Step on the turf and if the leaf blade bounces back up, your lawn is in good shape.' (context:span:15) suggests 'turf' is the ground cover. It is unclear if 'turf' is an alias for 'grass', 'lawn', or both. Given the mention of 'leaf blade', it is strongly associated with 'grass'.

The phrases 'different types of grasses' (context:span:2) and 'The type of grass you have' (context:span:7) both refer to categories of grass. It's unclear if these are distinct concepts or just variations in phrasing for the same idea of grass categorization.

The phrase 'what type of fertilizer you need to use' (context:span:7) implies a categorization of fertilizer. It's not explicitly defined as a separate entity from 'Fertilizer' itself, but rather a distinction of it.

The text refers to 'lawn' as an area to measure (context:span:12) and whose condition can be assessed (context:span:15). 'Grass' refers to the plant itself. It is unclear if a 'lawn' is an area *covered by* grass, or if 'lawn' is simply another term for 'grass' in this context. The mention of 'leaf blade' in relation to 'lawn' suggests a close connection.
